title: Why One Farnesyl Tail Is Usually Not Enough

scenes.tts: Ras has no segment crossing the membrane, yet it works at the membrane's inner face. What keeps it there? The puzzle has two parts. A lipid must join the protein, and that lipid must remain in a bilayer.
scenes.caption: Ras has no segment crossing the membrane, yet it works at the membrane's inner face. What keeps it there? The puzzle has two parts. A lipid must join the protein, and that lipid must remain in a bilayer.
scenes.visual: COLOR MAP for both films: proteins blue, lipid tails yellow, positive charge red, address lipids green, enzymes purple. Fill the frame with a plasma-membrane cross-section labelled cytosol below. Keep a small on-screen label, schematic, throughout the carried cartoon world. A large blue Ras block approaches but has no transmembrane segment. A yellow tail joins Ras, then points toward the bilayer. Keep the question visible while the tail gently swings. No molecular structures.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the carried membrane world: Why One Farnesyl Tail Is Usually Not Enough. Ras and its yellow tail continue a slow drift.

scenes.tts: First, separate two interactions that students often mix up. A covalent bond joins the lipid to the protein. A much weaker, non-covalent contact holds the lipid tail in the bilayer. The covalent bond can last while the tail repeatedly enters and leaves membranes. Permanent attachment to Ras does not mean permanent membrane binding.

scenes.tts: Watch one farnesyl tail sample the membrane and release. What should happen if Ras gains a compatible second contact? Will its visits remain brief, or become much longer?
scenes.caption: Watch one farnesyl tail sample the membrane and release. What should happen if Ras gains a compatible second contact? Will its visits remain brief, or become much longer?
scenes.visual: One blue Ras block samples the same membrane three times. Each short visit leaves a fading tick on a schematic time strip. A question mark occupies the empty second-contact slot.
scenes.narration: Watch one farnesyl tail sample the membrane and release. What should happen if Ras gains a compatible second contact? Will its visits remain brief, or become much longer?

scenes.visual: Hold the question and time strip. Ras continues slow sampling motion, but no answer appears.

scenes.tts: The visits become longer. Both contacts must release together before the protein escapes. That coincidence is rarer. A second lipid can provide that contact. So can a positive patch attracted to negative lipids on the membrane's inner face.
scenes.caption: The visits become longer. Both contacts must release together before the protein escapes. That coincidence is rarer. A second lipid can provide that contact. So can a positive patch attracted to negative lipids on the membrane's inner face.
scenes.visual: Transform the question slot first into a second yellow tail, then into a red positive patch facing sparse minus signs. In both cases, the visit tick stretches across most of the schematic time strip. Motion continues as each contact flexes independently.
scenes.narration: The visits become longer. Both contacts must release together before the protein escapes. That coincidence is rarer. A second lipid can provide that contact. So can a positive patch attracted to negative lipids on the membrane's inner face.

scenes.tts: H Ras and N Ras use farnesyl plus palmitate. K Ras four B uses farnesyl plus a lysine-rich positive patch. In both, farnesyl supplies the first contact. These are not identical addresses. They are two ways to combine membrane contact with another signal.
scenes.caption: H-Ras and N-Ras use farnesyl plus palmitate. K-Ras4B uses farnesyl plus a lysine-rich positive patch. In both, farnesyl supplies the first contact. These are not identical addresses. They are two ways to combine membrane contact with another signal.
scenes.visual: Split the carried view into two large cases without changing positions. Left: two separate blue blocks: N-Ras with a farnesyl tail and a palmitate tail, and H-Ras with a farnesyl tail and two palmitate tails (three yellow tails in all). Right: blue K-Ras4B with one yellow tail and a red plus patch. Labels slide into place; do not draw atoms or bonds.
scenes.narration: H-Ras and N-Ras use farnesyl plus palmitate. K-Ras4B uses farnesyl plus a lysine-rich positive patch. In both, farnesyl supplies the first contact. These are not identical addresses. They are two ways to combine membrane contact with another signal.

scenes.tts: Why is the change so large? Favorable free-energy contributions add. The equilibrium effect grows exponentially, not step by step. This is a thermodynamic effect, not a new covalent bond. A computed curve shows how a modest extra contribution can greatly raise the share of time on the membrane.

scenes.tts: The second contact also creates control. Remove palmitate, or weaken a positive patch, and the strong hold becomes weak again. That is a switch in location. The protein can leave without breaking its permanent farnesyl attachment.

scenes.visual: Return to the two cases. On the left, the second yellow tail detaches from H-Ras. On the right, the red positive patch fades. Both blue proteins resume membrane sampling while each yellow farnesyl tail remains firmly attached to its protein.

scenes.tts: Palmitate is especially useful because cells can remove and replace it. It goes on mainly at the Golgi, and it can come off on any membrane. Farnesyl remains attached while palmitate changes whether H Ras is tightly trapped or loosely sampling membranes. The same protein changes residence without losing farnesyl.

scenes.visual: Follow one large blue H-Ras block through a looping schematic cell view. A purple enzyme adds a second yellow tail near a labelled Golgi. H-Ras rides on a moving vesicle toward the plasma membrane. The tail later comes off; H-Ras samples internal membranes. Mark the entire loop schematic.

scenes.tts: This is the grip half of the lesson's rule. Lipids control signaling protein location by supplying grip, address, or both. The rule applies within this membrane-targeting scope. Here, the second signal converts a brief encounter into regulated membrane residence.

scenes.visual: The loop compresses back into the original membrane world. Large words grip and address appear; grip brightens while address remains outlined for later. H-Ras alternates between a short one-contact visit and a long two-contact residence.

scenes.tts: So ask three questions about any lipid-modified protein. Which contact puts it on membranes? Which additional signal strengthens or directs that contact? And what can remove or oppose it? The answers predict both localization and the switch that can change it.
